items.prompt:
Which sentence does NOT belong in a paragraph about cats?
A) Cats purr when they are happy.
B) Cats sleep about 12-16 hours a day.
C) My favorite movie is about a dog.
D) Cats use their whiskers to sense their surroundings.

steps: C is about a dog movie and has nothing to do with cats.

items.prompt:
What does it mean to REVISE your writing?
A) Fix spelling errors
B) Add capital letters
C) Improve your ideas, add details, and remove off-topic sentences
D) Count the number of sentences

steps: Revising focuses on improving the content: adding details, removing off-topic parts, and making ideas clearer. Fixing spelling and capitals is editing.

items.prompt: Read: 'I like apples. Apples are red. My dog is named Spot. Apples are crunchy.' Which sentence is off-topic?
items.answer: 'My dog is named Spot.' It has nothing to do with apples.

steps: The topic is apples. The sentence about the dog does not connect to apples.

items.prompt: Revise this weak sentence by adding one specific detail: 'We saw animals at the zoo.'
items.answer: Sample: 'We saw a family of gorillas at the zoo, and the baby gorilla sat on its mother's back and watched us with curious dark eyes.'

steps: Ask: WHAT animals? WHAT did they do? Add a specific detail.

items.prompt:
Which is a STRONGER sentence?
A) 'I ate food.'
B) 'I ate a warm bowl of tomato soup with a grilled cheese sandwich that oozed melted cheddar.'
items.answer: B — it includes specific, vivid details about what was eaten.

steps: Specific details make writing more interesting and help the reader picture what happened.

items.prompt: A student wrote: 'My sister is nice. She helps me sometimes. I have a green backpack. She always shares with me.' Which sentence should be removed?
items.answer: 'I have a green backpack.' It is off-topic — the paragraph is about the student's sister.

steps: Every sentence should connect to the main topic (the student's sister). The backpack sentence does not.

items.prompt: What does it mean to EDIT your writing? Give two examples of things you check when editing.
items.answer: Editing means fixing small errors. Examples: checking for correct capitalization of names and the start of sentences, checking for end punctuation (period, question mark), and fixing misspelled words.

steps: Editing is fixing mechanics: spelling, capitalization, and punctuation. It is different from revising, which improves ideas.

items.prompt: Revise this sentence to make it more detailed: 'The game was exciting.'
items.answer: Sample: 'The game was so exciting that I jumped out of my chair when our team scored the winning point with only two seconds left on the clock.'

steps: Add details: WHAT game? WHY was it exciting? WHAT happened?

items.prompt: Read this paragraph: 'Snow is amazing. It is cold and white. My favorite color is purple. You can build snowmen and go sledding with snow.' Which sentence is off-topic?
items.answer: 'My favorite color is purple.' It does not connect to snow.

steps: The topic is snow. Favorite colors are unrelated.

items.prompt: True or False: Revising means you are fixing spelling mistakes. Explain your answer.
items.answer: False. Revising means improving the content of your writing — adding details, removing off-topic sentences, and making ideas clearer. Fixing spelling is editing.

steps: Revising = improve ideas and content. Editing = fix spelling, punctuation, capitalization.

items.prompt: Read: 'I think school is important. Learning helps your brain grow. I had pasta for lunch. Students learn reading, math, and science.' Which sentence should be removed?
items.answer: 'I had pasta for lunch.' It is off-topic — the paragraph is about the importance of school.

steps: The paragraph is about school being important. Lunch is not related.

items.prompt: Revise this weak ending sentence for a narrative about winning a spelling bee: 'I won and went home.'
items.answer: Sample: 'I clutched my first-place ribbon on the whole bus ride home, still dizzy with happiness, replaying the moment my name was called in my head over and over.'

steps: A good ending shows a feeling and reflects on the moment. It should not just state an action.

items.prompt:
Which question should you ask when REVISING your writing?
A) Did I spell all the words correctly?
B) Did I use capital letters at the start of sentences?
C) Is every sentence on the topic? Can I add more details?
D) Did I put a period at the end of each sentence?

steps: Questions about spelling, capitals, and punctuation are for editing. Revision questions focus on content and ideas.

items.prompt: Improve this sentence by replacing the underlined vague word with something specific: 'The dog made a sound.'
items.answer: Sample: 'The dog let out a sharp, high-pitched yelp.'

steps: 'Made a sound' is too vague. Replace with a specific sound word like yelped, barked, howled, or whimpered.

items.prompt: Look at this paragraph: 'Exercise is good for you. It makes your body strong. I have two brothers. Exercise also helps your brain work better.' Identify the off-topic sentence AND revise the paragraph to fix it.
items.answer: Off-topic: 'I have two brothers.' Revised: 'Exercise is good for you in many ways. It makes your body stronger and helps your heart and lungs work better. Exercise also helps your brain focus and remember information more easily.'

steps: Revise to make the remaining sentences stronger and more specific.
